Circular genome visualizations are essential for exploring structural variants and gene regulation.
Existing tools often require complex scripting and manual configuration, making the process time-consuming, error-prone, and difficult to learn.
We introduce AuraGenome, a large language model (LLM)-powered framework for rapid, reusable, and scalable generation of multilayered circular genome visualizations.
AuraGenome combines a semantic-driven multiagent workflow with an interactive visual analytics system.

The workflow employs seven specialized LLM-driven agents, each assigned distinct roles, such as intent recognition, layout planning, and code generation, to transform raw genomic data into tailored visualizations.
The system supports multiple coordinated views tailored for genomic data, offering ring, radial, and chord-based layouts to represent multilayered circular genome visualizations.
The system enables interactions and configuration reuse.
The system supports realtime refinement and high-quality report export.
We validate its effectiveness through two case studies and a comprehensive user study.
AuraGenome is available at https://github.com/Darius18/AuraGenome.

Three representative layout strategies for circular genome visualizations are formalized: ring (concentric stacking of feature tracks), radial (center-out projection), and chord (arc-based linking of genomic loci).
These layouts can be selected, composed, and refined interactively through novel interface elements, such as the parameter panel and sequence log.
The parameter panel and sequence log enable visual code reuse, stepwise branching, and traceable generation history.

$E _ { A }$ aimed to investigate chromosomal translocation patterns in AML.

A curated dataset of chromosomal translocations was uploaded by $E _ { A }$.

A chord layout was selected by $E _ { A }$ to visualize interchromosomal associations.

$E _ { A }$ incorporated a second dataset containing gene expression profiles.

We created a visualization tool, called Circos, to facilitate the identification and analysis of similarities and differences arising from comparisons of genomes.
Circos is effective in displaying variation in genome structure and any other kind of positional relationships between genomic intervals.
Such data are routinely produced by sequence alignments, hybridization arrays, genome mapping, and genotyping studies.

Circos uses a circular ideogram layout to facilitate the display of relationships between pairs of positions by the use of ribbons, which encode the position, size, and orientation of related genomic elements.
Circos is capable of displaying data as scatter, line and histogram plots, heat maps, tiles, connectors and text.
Bitmap or vector images can be created from GFF-style data inputs and hierarchical configuration files, which can be easily generated by automated tools.
This makes Circos suitable for rapid deployment in data analysis and reporting pipelines.
Circos is licensed under GPL and available at http://mkweb.bcgsc.ca/circos.
An interactive online version of Circos designed to visualize tabular data can be found at http://mkweb.bcgsc.ca/circos/tableviewer.

Advances in speed, quality, and affordability of whole genome analysis, including genome sequencing, have transitioned the comparative genomics field from comparing reference sequence assemblies to comparing assemblies of individual genomes.
Inter-species analysis leverages information about one species to further the understanding of biological mechanisms in another.
Comparative methods are now used to discover differences between individuals.
These differences affect individuals' response to the environment, such as susceptibility to disease and responsiveness to therapy.
The ability to collect enormous amounts of sequence information is outpacing the rate of developing new methods to store, process, analyze, and visualize these data.
New approaches in data modeling and analysis need corresponding innovations in data visualization.
Detecting, filtering, and classifying patterns within large datasets require instructive and clear visualizations.
Effective visualizations should adapt to the density and dynamic range of the data.
Effective visualizations should maintain complexity and detail in the data.
Effective visualizations should scale well without sacrificing clarity and specificity.

The application of a germane data representation and its corresponding visualization to a domain-specific problem has historically improved the effectiveness of data presentation, analysis, and dissemination.
In some cases, the benefit of a new approach has altered how data are perceived and investigated.
Tree maps have been applied to show distribution of disk usage on a file system (Johnson and Shneiderman 1991) and hierarchical biological data (McConnell et al. 2002).
Directed graphs have been used to depict networks, pathways, and phylogenetic information (Ciccarelli et al. 2006; Darwin 1859; Letunic and Bork 2007).
Clustered heat maps have been used to visualize array and expression data (Eisen et al. 1998; Sneath 1957).
Effective visualizations exemplify virtues such as clarity, a high data-to-ink ratio (Tufte 1992), and favorable scaling characteristics.
These visualization approaches have been widely adopted because they addressed pressing visualization problems within domains where data sets were previously opaque to effective visual inspection.
A pressing visualization problem exists in the domain of comparative genomics, specifically in the comparative genomics of individuals.
A visual paradigm is needed to display relationships between genomes to leverage large amounts of sequence data and expand the power of personal genomics.
Previous efforts to visualize positional relationships used linearly arranged ideograms connected by lines to represent rearrangements.
One approach uses encoding in HSL (hue, saturation, lightness) color space to perform three-way comparisons.
The methods in these approaches are effective for illustrating local alignments between similar sequences.

The shortcoming of the linear layout becomes apparent in representations associating many ideograms with numerous relationships, where multitudes of lines transgress unrelated ideograms and make patterns difficult to discern.
Color maps are used to mitigate overburdened visualizations by mapping a position pair onto a position and a color.
Color maps reduce the texture and richness of the data despite addressing the problem of overburdened visualizations.
Circularly arranged ideograms are prevalent in visualizations of microbial genomes, which are circular.
At least one report combined paired-position data with a circular layout to show relationships between genomic positions, specifically pathways.
The report hinted at the benefit of adopting the circular layout for application to structural data.
The challenge in displaying large volumes of genomic rearrangement data is addressed.

Visual representations based on circular shapes are frequently used in visualization applications.
Circos plots in bioinformatics bend graphs into a wheel of information with connective lines running through the center like spokes.
Circos plots result in aesthetically appealing and impressive visualizations that fit long data sequences into a small quadratic space.
Visualization researchers generally advise against making visualizations with radial layouts.
There is evidence that circular layouts are preferable in some cases.
There is no clear evidence for what layout is preferable for matrices and connective data in particular, which are common data types in circos plots.
A user study was performed to compare circular and linear layouts.
The tasks in the user study are inspired by genomics data.
The results of the user study generalize to many other application areas involving comparison and connective data.

Empirical evidence is contributed on the suitedness of linear versus circular layouts.

The case study confirms the utility of Gosling and provides guidance on suitable areas for future development.

Circular graph layouts can be attractive for visualization designers.
Bending the main axis into a circular shape is convenient for fitting long data sequences into a quadratic space.
Genomics and bioinformatics data often consist of long sequences, which could be one explanation why circular plots are common in these domains.
The high screen-space density is further articulated for connective data, also common in genomics, which can be represented as connective lines inside the circle in a spoke-like manner.
Other reasons for choosing circular layouts could be that they are considered aesthetically appealing and innovative compared to a traditional linear alternative.
Visualization designs should primarily be evaluated on how well they support the analysis task at hand.

Circular layouts are used for a multitude of datatypes, including matrix data, which consists of rows and columns of scalar values, and connective data, which consists of a sequence of positions and interconnections between the positions.
Comparisons between circular and linear plots have been made for other settings.
We have not found studies comparing circular and linear plots for connective data and matrix data, which are two data types of particular relevance for genomics.
The main contribution of the work is an empirical study on the suitability of circular and linear layouts for comparative tasks with matrix and connective data.
The visualization challenge initially comes from genomics applications.

The circular layouts in genomics data are typically one or more tracks arranged in parallel or serially, often with interconnections running through the circle’s center, creating a chord diagram.
Circular visualizations, also called radial, have attracted substantial research attention outside of genomics-specific work.
Radial charts are often used for temporal data due to their cyclical nature.
Previous efforts have compared two layouts from different angles.
A comparison of smartwatch visualization designs for regular bar charts, donut charts, and radial bar charts found that the radial visualization performed the worst.
Performance of an area estimation task has been shown to be similar for circles and rectangles.
Goldberg and Helfman evaluated linear versus radial bar, line, area, and scatterplots, outlining how scanning patterns differed.
Goldberg and Helfman recommended that not too many concentric rings be used in a radial graph due to risk of confusion.
In the genomics setting, adding more tracks to a circular layout makes the individual tracks very small.
In the genomics setting, if tracks are long, part of the circle ends up out of the viewport.
Dielh et al. [DBB10] evaluated the performance of radial and linear layouts of matrix data for tasks requiring navigation and comparison of elements.
The results indicated that it is easier to remember positions in a radial coordinate system than a cartesian one.
There are reading direction effects for the cartesian layout.
Task completion times for correct answers were significantly faster for the cartesian layout.
The study complements the linear versus circular comparisons by investigating previously unchartered territory.
Empirical evidence is provided for the suitability of linear and circular layouts for two data types.
The two data types are matrix data (multiple stacked tracks) and connective data.

The taxonomy by Nusrat et al. [NHG19] concerns visualization tasks in genomics.
The taxonomy by Nusrat et al. [NHG19] is an extension and adaptation of the more generic taxonomy of Brehmer et al. [BM13].
The taxonomy of Brehmer et al. [BM13] disentangles the motives from the means and the goal by dividing the tasks into why, how, and what.
Andrienko and Andrienko [AA06] categorize tasks as elementary or synoptic.
Synoptic tasks relate to trends and tendencies of a reference set.
Elementary tasks pertain only to one element.
The difficulty of a comparison task depends on the number of items, item size and complexity, and the size and complexity of the relationship between items.
Gleicher et al. outline three strategies for comparison: scanning sequentially, scanning subsets, and summarizing somehow.
The layout of the visualization can affect its effectiveness.
Gleicher et al. identify the layout of visualizations as an area for future research.
L’Yi et al. conducted a survey on comparative visualization arrangements.
L’Yi et al. suggested design principles for using juxtaposition, superposition, and explicit encoding for visualizations aimed at comparative tasks.
Ondov et al. compared different arrangements for data analysis.
Ondov et al. found they were not able to extract specific guidelines per datatype.
Ondov et al. called for more empirical studies on different datasets and tasks.
Both data and task type affect what layout choices are appropriate.
Layout needs to be considered to ensure the effectiveness of the visualization.

DNA is present in nearly every cell in the human body.
DNA is composed of four bases: A, C, T, and G.
The bases are attached to a strand made of sugar.
A specific base is referred to by its chromosome and the position it has on that chromosome.
For example, Chr3:310478 refers to the 310478th base on chromosome three.
Humans have mostly the same bases in the same positions but there are variations.
When a base is different than the reference genome, this is called a variant or a mutation.
Variants are frequent in cancer.
A cancer sample has both tumor cells and healthy cells.
Only a percentage of the sample will have a variation that is specific to the tumor cells.

The abstraction of the task is pattern matching between rows, specifically to find a row where a fraction of another row’s values has been added.

The second task was to determine for a specified chromosome which other chromosome it had the most interactions with.

This study briefly explored the possibility of displaying genomics data without having genomic position on any axis.
A contamination visualization with variant IDs on one axis independent of their genomic position was introduced.
The contamination visualization represents a first step toward displaying genomics data without genomic position on any axis.
There are interesting visualization opportunities in displaying genomics data without genomic position on any axis.
A user study was performed comparing linear and circular layouts for two comparative tasks inspired by genomics.
For matrix data, the linear layout led to higher accuracy.
For interconnection data, there was no difference in accuracy between linear and circular layouts.
For both datatypes, the results weakly indicate that the linear layout resulted in shorter task completion times.
The study contributes a strengthened and expanded understanding of when linear layouts are preferable over circular ones.
The study contributes an evaluation of the Gosling grammar as a tool for rapid prototyping.

Interpretation of genomics data relies on the application of a wide range of visualization tools.
A large number of visualization techniques for genomics data and different analysis tasks pose a significant challenge for analysts.
Genomics analysts often base their visualization choices on trial and error or technical details, such as data formats that a specific tool can load.
This approach prevents genomics analysts from making effective visualization choices for the many combinations of data types and analysis questions they encounter.
Visualization recommendation systems assist non-experts in creating data visualizations by recommending appropriate visualizations based on the data and task characteristics.
Existing visualization recommendation systems are not designed to handle domain-specific problems.
GenoREC is a novel visualization recommendation system for genomics.
GenoREC enables genomics analysts to select effective visualizations based on a description of their data and analysis tasks.
The recommendation model in GenoREC uses a knowledge-based method for choosing appropriate visualizations.
GenoREC includes a web application that enables analysts to input their requirements, explore recommended visualizations, and export them for their usage.
Two user studies demonstrate that GenoREC recommends visualizations accepted by domain experts and suited to address the given genomics analysis problem.

The almost ubiquitous availability of genomic data has revolutionized research in biology and medicine.
Interpreting genomic and epigenomic data can improve our understanding of the genetic causes and mechanisms that underlie common and rare diseases.
Visualization plays a central role in the analysis of genomic data as an efficient approach for data exploration and knowledge communication.
A large number of visualization techniques and tools have been developed over the years to meet the wide variety of analysis requirements in the field of genomics.
To succeed in the visual analysis of genomics data, a genomics analyst or a domain user must carefully select suitable visualizations based on data characteristics and analysis tasks.
Genomics analysts currently use visualizations based on their prior experience or out-of-the-box visualizations generated by popular genome browsers.
Many visualizations used in genomics do not consider appropriate visualization best practices, results from empirical studies, or theoretical guidance.
Circos, a widely used visualization technique in genomics, uses a radial layout with length or position channels that represent quantitative features.
The radial layout used by Circos is found to be inaccurate and inefficient in data interpretation.
Commonly used genome browser tools lack effective multi-scale designs, such as overviews and detail views, as shown by survey results on genomics tools.
Ineffective and, in many cases, wrong visual designs can result from limitations in common and specialized visualization approaches in genomics.
The limitations of current visualization approaches in genomics indicate a need for better visualization guidance.
Visualization researchers have contributed many visualization recommendation systems, spanning general to domain-specific systems.
Existing visualization recommendation systems suggest a data visualization primarily based on the data.
In very few cases, existing systems also consider the user’s tasks.
These systems allow data analysts who are not experts in visualization design to focus on the analysis of data.
These systems offload the work of visualization design to an algorithm.
Existing systems are typically designed only for common visualization types, such as bar charts, line charts, and scatter plots.
Existing systems cannot be applied to scenarios which require complex or domain-specific visual encodings.
The design space of genomics visualizations is different from a taxonomy of general visualization.

The design space of genomics visualizations includes unique combinations of visualizations rarely used in other fields, such as radial overview visualizations and complex glyph encodings for gene structures.
Analyzing large-scale genomic data requires multiple coordinated views.
Existing visualization recommendation systems focus on single-view visualizations.
The analysis tasks in genomics are domain-specific and not considered in other visualization recommendations.
GenoREC is a novel recommendation system for interactive genomic data visualizations based on specifications about data and tasks.
The core contribution of GenoREC is a knowledge-based recommendation model consisting of a set of decision rules summarized from empirical knowledge and published visualization practices.
The recommendation of individual visualizations is decomposed into six design components based on the taxonomy proposed by Nusrat et al. [38].
For each design component, the design space is enumerated and rules are crafted to describe the design decisions.
A web application is contributed that allows genomics data analysts to describe their data and task specifications and explore the corresponding recommended visualizations.
The output of GenoREC is a specification for Gosling, a grammar-based genomics visualization toolkit.
The specification can be used by genomics analysts to customize the recommended visualization for further use.
This work primarily focuses on the evaluation of GenoREC’s recommendation model.
The results of the user study demonstrate that GenoREC’s recommendations are helpful for analysts working in the space of genomics data analysis.
Visualization recommendation systems consider four factors: data characteristics, task orientation, domain knowledge, and user preference.
Data characteristics involve identifying visual encodings corresponding to the data type of attributes.
Mackinlay’s APT system was one of the first systems to implement automatic mapping from data characteristics to 2D graphics or charts.
Polaris, the research prototype of Tableau, used APT’s mapping of data characteristics to visual encoding to recommend visualizations.
The Sage system extended the concept of automatic mapping of data variables to visualization by supporting more types of visual encoding.
Voyager and Draco are recent systems developed to facilitate data-based visualization recommendations.
Draco contributes a technique to learn recommendation knowledge from existing empirical studies.
Task-oriented recommendations prioritize a user’s intentions behind visualizing data as the main criteria for recommending visualizations.
Current task-oriented recommendation systems support domain-independent low-level analytical tasks, such as compare and summarize.
Domain knowledge imposes restrictions on recommendation system results, as domain experts may prefer familiar or widely accepted visualizations.
GEViT-Rec focuses on epidemiology and recommends visually coherent chart combinations by inferring a data source graph and mapping it to view templates.
User preference involves factoring end users’ preferences into the recommendation system output.
Draco includes a method to factor user preferences in the form of user-defined constraints.
GenoREC incorporates data, task, and domain-specific guidelines for recommending visualizations.
Visualization recommendation systems can be categorized based on their recommendation method: data-driven and knowledge-based.
Data-driven systems recommend visualizations for the given input data by learning from a large number of visualization examples.
A variety of machine learning models have been employed to learn from a collection of examples, including neural networks, reinforcement learning, and decision trees.
VizML uses a neural network to learn visualization design choices from a large corpus of datasets paired with visualizations.
Table2charts employs a reinforcement learning framework to learn step-by-step visualization constructions from a large corpus of tables paired with charts.
Knowledge-based systems recommend visualizations by following a set of expert-defined rules and constraints, making the rules more interpretable compared to data-driven approaches.
These rules are usually formalized based on the properties of data, such as trends or outliers, and the effectiveness of visual encodings.
The 'Show Me' feature of Tableau provides automatic mark selection based on the data properties type, role, and interpretation.
Voyager and Voyager2 rank encodings based on a set of perceptual effectiveness metrics.
The multivariate network (MVN) wizard recommends visualizations based on a ranking generated by visualization experts.
There is work on the recommendation of layouts for multi-view visualizations.
Kristiansen et al. present an approach that allows semantic alignment of multiple views based on the content of visualizations, such as visual channels used.
Data-driven recommendation systems have demonstrated reasonable performance.
Data-driven recommendation systems usually require many high-quality examples.
High-quality examples are generally not available for domain-specific problems.
Knowledge-based recommendation systems can remedy the problem of limited high-quality examples.
It is possible to develop a recommendation model using existing knowledge and best practices from the information visualization field and domain theory.
GenoREC uses a knowledge-based visualization recommendation model.
The GenoREC model is based on a survey of genomics visualizations.
The GenoREC model combines design principles from visualization literature.
There are several resources that can assist genomics analysts in choosing an appropriate visualization technique.
Nusrat et al. surveyed over a hundred genomics visualization tools.
Nusrat et al. proposed a taxonomy for genomic visualization based on datasets, visual encodings, and tasks.
The paper by Nusrat et al. serves as a theoretical resource for analysts to decide an appropriate visualization technique.
GenoCAT and awesome-genome-visualization are databases of existing genomic data visualization tools and techniques.
These databases are valuable resources for analysts who want to identify relevant techniques to visualize data.
These galleries are exploratory and do not prescribe or suggest visualization designs to the users.
In the case of genomics, exploratory tools may have limited use because experts often lack formal training to judge if the suggested options are adequate visualizations.
The proposed GenoREC system recommends visualization designs that are accurate from a visualization theory standpoint.
The proposed GenoREC system recommends visualization designs that are appropriate for the given data and task requirements.

This section provides an overview of the genome-mapped datasets.
The section includes tasks with abstractions to support discussions throughout the paper.
The human genome is a hierarchical structure.
A genome consists of one or multiple chromosomes.
Chromosomes are subdivided into smaller regions called genes (feature sets or features).
At the lowest level of hierarchy, genomes are composed of building blocks called nucleotides (A, C, G, and T).
The hierarchical structure makes it possible to measure data at different granularities.
Data can be recorded at the individual nucleotide level, known as point granularity (e.g., single nucleotide polymorphisms, or SNP, that covers only one nucleotide).
Data can also be measured at a gene level, leading to a segment granularity dataset (e.g., genes whose protein-coding regions cover more than one nucleotide).
The density of information varies for genomes.
In some experiments, data is recorded for each nucleotide, leading to a contiguous data density (e.g., DNA conservation scores, which are generally available for each position in a genome).
In other cases, the data may be sparse (e.g., genes that only cover a relatively small proportion of the genome), leading to empty and missing values.
Genome datasets can include network-based data and spatially mapped data.
Network data in genomes generally represent connectivity between distant regions of a genome (e.g., physical interactions between different locations in the folded genome).
Network data may also represent connectivity between two different genomes (e.g., synteny).
The type of data recorded for genomes, also called expression levels, can be three main abstract types: quantitative, categorical, and text.
In genomics, textual annotations (e.g., 'BRCA2' gene) are important and are distinguished from categorical data, being visualized as textual representations.
More information on parallels between features in genomics data and other domain data (e.g., geospatial data) can be found in a survey paper [38].
Genomics researchers perform analytical tasks with data visualizations to explore genomic features and answer critical domain questions.
A review of genomics visualization tasks can be found in the survey by Nusrat et al. [38].
Through a thematic analysis of the tasks in the survey using the multi-level task typology of Brehmer & Munzner [6], genomics analysis tasks were categorized into three low-level query tasks.
The 'Identify' task involves analyzing features in a genomic region of interest to read a specific feature value.
For the 'Identify' task, an example is navigating to a gene A and checking its expression level.
The 'Compare' task involves comparing features located in multiple genomic regions.
For the 'Compare' task, an example is comparing the gene expression level between gene A and gene B.

The 'Overview' task involves looking at a larger genomic region or a whole genome to get an overview of the attributes of a feature set and identify interesting patterns such as outliers, clusters, or trends.
For the 'Overview' task, an example is identifying regions with many mutations.
The tasks and data introduced in this section play a critical role in the design of the GenoREC system.
GenoREC recommends linear and circular layouts when a user specifies a BED file and a VCF file with categorical data.
GenoREC switches to a linear recommendation when a user adds a BIGWIG file with quantitative data.
A use-case scenario is presented to illustrate how GenoREC enables analysts to find appropriate visualization recommendations.
This scenario is also presented in the supplementary video.
Ada is a genomics researcher working at a cancer research institute.
Ada wants to develop a visualization to analyze genetic data obtained from three different files: a BED file, a VCF file, and a BIGWIG file.
The BED1 file stores the location of genes linked with certain diseases.
The VCF1 file stores structural variant events of a cancer patient.
The BIGWIG1 file stores protein interactions with DNA.
Ada wants to compare the quantitative values of the BIGWIG file between different regions.
Ada wants to understand if specific genetic features in BED1 and VCF1 tracks contribute to the measurement of the BIGWIG file.
Ada visualizes the data using conventional genomics visualization tools such as UCSC Genome Browser, IGV Browser, and WashU Epigenome Browser.
Conventional genomics visualization tools can create visuals for specific data types.
Ada is unable to use a single tool to look at all her data and combine different file types for integrated analysis.
Ada spends a lot of time working across tools and makes compromises on her analyses.
Conventional tools are tightly coupled with default visualization techniques.
Ada would like to explore alternative visualization techniques and easily customize her visualizations.
Conventional tools do not consider Ada’s task, placing a burden on her to follow design guidelines to identify the best encoding.
Without task guidance, Ada may choose a misleading visualization.
Ada decides to try GenoREC to get a recommendation for a visualization that supports her requirements and steers her towards the final plots.
The user interface of GenoREC consists of two main panels.
The left panel is a domain-centric data and task elicitation interface.
The data and task specification panel contains two parts: data description and tasks.
The right panel is a visualization gallery that displays recommended visualizations.
The system automatically defines 'Connection' based on the file format.
The system recommends two tracks stacked in a linear and circular layout (Fig. 3A).
The recommended visualizations allow an overview of the genetic features from the two files.
The genetic features are visually aligned on the same genomic axis to help concurrent analysis.
Ada adds a BIGWIG file description.
The updated recommendation removes the circular layout recommendation and shows two linear tracks.
The first linear track option uses a bar mark for the quantitative data.
The second linear track option uses a line mark for the same quantitative data (Fig. 3B).
Both visualizations support looking up high and low values of the BIGWIG file.
Both visualizations support analyzing genes in the corresponding BED and VCF tracks.
GenoREC was developed through an iterative design process.
Existing literature in recommendation systems and genomics visualization, including genomics visualization tasks, was analyzed to identify an initial set of system design goals.
A formative study was conducted with five domain experts to solicit feedback on the recommendation output, user interface, and system workflow.
Experts were interviewed to understand their genomics visualization authoring process and current challenges.
None of the experts involved in the studies are authors of this paper.

Input from experts and common design suggestions from prior work on general recommender systems and visualization recommendation systems were combined to identify goals for further development of GenoREC.
The recommended visualization should be familiar to users in the genomics field.
Swearingen and Sinha found that familiar output increases trust within the recommendation model.
During the interviews, the experts emphasized that recommendations should be familiar and easy to understand.
Genomics visualizations have unique characteristics that differentiate them from common visualizations outside genomics.
It is a general practice to arrange data attributes available in genomics datasets as parallel tracks.
Experts noted that it might require additional effort to understand and communicate the results of an unfamiliar visualization technique or design.
The system should consider best practices from visualization design and the domain to recommend the visualization.
A core principle for existing visualization recommendation systems is mapping the data and, in some cases, task requirements to effective visualization designs.
The system should leverage the knowledge generated by the visualization community through empirical and theoretical research to build rules that guide the recommendation of visualizations.
In addition to the general visualization guidelines, the system should also consider domain-specific knowledge for the recommendation.
Heatmaps are common in genomics.
It is known that the color channel is not optimal for displaying quantitative values.
The system should ensure that domain practices are not eliminated from the recommendation.
The system should support common file formats and tasks used for the analysis of genomics data.
The BED, VCF, and BIGWIG file formats are discussed in Sect. 4.
Experts noted that the ability to specify data requirements in familiar file formats could reduce the learning curve associated with the system.
The system should support file formats that accommodate common data types and structures available in genomics.
The recommendation system should enable users to steer the recommendation progressively.
Users may come to a recommendation system when they are not sure what they want and need assistance to find an item of interest.
Users may need methods to interact with recommendation inputs in a flexible way and update them until they find an item of interest.
To support flexible updates, the interface needs to support a quick turnaround time in showing the recommended outputs.
The design of the system should account for users changing between different data and task inputs.
The system should analyze the change in the visualization recommendation output based on the inputs.
Alternative designs of the same data should be recommended to analysts.
The design space of genomics visualization is large.
Users may only have familiarity with a small subset of visualizations within the larger design space.
The system should recommend design alternatives to users whenever it is possible.
Options can improve the trust in the system.
Options may lead to serendipitous discoveries.
Serendipitous discoveries may lead to a positive attitude towards a recommendation system.
GenoREC is a novel visualization recommendation system for the analysis of genomics data.
The GenoREC system design and recommendation workflow are summarized in Fig. 1 (Bottom).
GenoREC consists of a front-end user interface that allows users to specify their input requirements to the system.
The front-end user interface of GenoREC allows users to browse the recommended visualizations.
The back-end recommendation model of GenoREC generates visualization recommendations.
The back-end recommendation model generates design configurations for appropriate visualizations given the user input.
The Input Compiler and Output Compiler modules orchestrate the exchange of information between the front-end and back-end.
A key design aspect of GenoREC is its modular architecture.
The modular architecture ensures that individual components are easy to update without affecting other system modules.
GenoREC’s user interface is implemented in JavaScript, HTML, and CSS.
The back-end recommendation model is published as a standalone JavaScript library on NPM.
GenoREC uses Gosling, a grammar-based visualization toolkit for genomics, for rendering recommendation.
GenoREC’s knowledge-based recommendation model recommends domain-specific visualizations based on visualization theory and best practices from the genomics domain.
The model is built on guidelines which map domain-specific input requirements to an appropriate output visualization.
The input and output space of GenoREC’s model is presented in this section.
The recommendation knowledge used by GenoREC is presented in this section.
The algorithm which allows the system to use the recommendation knowledge to generate the visualizations is described in this section.
The data input into GenoREC is divided into four categories: the assembly build, data type (quantitative, categorical, and text), feature set (feature extent and density), and connection.
The recommendation model expects the tasks (identify, compare, overview) as inputs.
The data and task input are discussed in Sect. 3.
GenoREC’s model breaks down the recommendation task into six intermediate steps: Encoding, Alignment, Layout, Partition, Arrangement, and Interactivity.
Each of these six components contains a set of possible output options as shown in Fig. 1B.
One of the main contributions of GenoREC is the use of sequential order to better reflect the dependencies between these components.
To determine the current order of components, we reviewed the genomics visualization taxonomy [38].
For each part of the taxonomy, we determined precursor steps.
We noticed that it was not possible to recommend an orthogonal 'Arrangement' if the 'Layout' of the tracks were circular.
This exercise allowed us to develop the sequence and led to the creation of the sequential model.
The sequential order of components ensures that the GenoREC system can accurately recommend visualizations.
We provide an overview of each component in the order GenoREC’s recommendation model determines them.
The encoding component identifies the visual mark and channel pair to encode attributes in a genomics dataset.
In genomics visualizations, there are four visual marks: point, line, rectangle ('rect'), and text.
There are also four channels: position, length, saturation, and hue.
The full list of combinations of marks and channels supported in GenoREC are visually depicted in Fig. 1B.
The alignment component identifies if the encodings from the Encoding component (C1) can be stacked or overlayed.
Stacked alignment applies encodings to individual tracks and then vertically stacks them.
A track refers to a unit visualization that corresponds to common visualization types.
Stacked alignment is used as the default option since it is the most frequent alignment in genomics visualizations.
Fig. 3A shows an example of stacked alignment where BED1 and VCF1 files are shown as two separate tracks that are vertically stacked.
The overlayed alignment merges encodings into a single track.
The Layout component selects the layout to display a track in the genomics visualization.
GenoREC supports three layouts: linear, circular, and space-filling.
The space-filling layout includes examples such as the Hilbert curve.
The partition component decides whether the chromosomes should be displayed in a contiguous track, where chromosomes are placed end-to-end.
The partition component decides whether the chromosomes should be displayed in a segregated manner, where each chromosome is independently displayed as a separate track.
Partition happens at a track level.
If a visualization has multiple tracks, GenoREC determines the division of each track.
The arrangement component is responsible for selecting the arrangement of multiple views.
In this paper, a view refers to a combination of one or multiple tracks.
Fig 3B represents two views, each consisting of two tracks from two data files.
The main difference between arrangement and partition is that arrangement is applied between views instead of between tracks.
In GenoREC, views with linear tracks can be arranged as parallel, adjacent, or orthogonal.
The orthogonal arrangement allows the creation of adjacency matrices for visualizing genomics data with a complete network connection between two sequences.
If views have a circular layout, GenoREC only permits parallel and adjacent arrangements.
The interactivity component is responsible for identifying proper interaction patterns for genomics visualization.
GenoREC supports two interaction patterns: coordinated interaction and focus+context.
In the coordinated interaction pattern, all tracks within a view have coordinated zooming and panning interactions.
The focus+context pattern allows users to focus on a specific portion of the genome while maintaining the context of the genome location.
This section presents the main design guidelines that shape the recommendation for GenoREC.
GenoREC uses best practices and domain-knowledge in combination (G2).
The selection of channels depends on the attribute types and low-level analytical tasks users want to perform with the visualization.
Experimental studies by Cleveland & McGill [9] and Heer & Bostock [15] ranked visual channels in terms of their accuracy to identify and compare quantitative data.
Based on the results of these studies, GenoREC maps quantitative values using position and length channels.
Fig. 5 shows the Decision Matrix for the Encoding component (C1).
Rows in the Decision Matrix represent the visual encodings.
Columns in the Decision Matrix represent the factors that affect the encoding selection.
A cell in the matrix with a value of 1 indicates that the encoding supports the factor.
An empty cell in the matrix represents a value of -1, indicating that the factor is not supported.
GenoREC allows mapping quantitative values of the color saturation channel for an overview task.
In overview tasks, users are looking for patterns, not individual values.
Color saturation can show variation in data for pattern search.
For categorical attributes, GenoREC uses categorical color schemes based on the ranking proposed by Mackinlay [30].
GenoREC supports overlayed alignments for genomics visualizations with multiple tracks only if the tracks are from the same file.
Overlaying tracks from different files can lead to occlusion due to the superposition of multiple marks at the same location.
GenoREC only supports overlaying position and color channels because they can co-exist without causing occlusion.
If a visualization has two tracks with position channels and one track with a color channel, GenoREC will combine the first position channel with the color channel.
This combination will lead to stacked and overlayed tracks.
In GenoREC, layouts are selected based on the input data and task descriptions, and the visual encoding set in the encoding component.
Waldner et al. [54] found that length and position channels make it easier to identify and compare visual representations in linear layouts.
This study recommends linear layouts when length and position are used in the encoding component for identifying and comparing tasks.
In overview tasks, where the user’s goal is to look for trends and patterns, GenoREC recommends both circular layouts and linear layouts.
GenoREC suggests parallel or orthogonal arrangements in linear layouts for inter-connectivity data.
Selection between parallel and orthogonal arrangements depends on the type of network data.
For dense networks, GenoREC recommends orthogonal arrangements.
For other cases, GenoREC recommends parallel arrangements.
For circular layouts, GenoREC recommends adjacent arrangements when there is a network connection.
Adjacent arrangements are one of the most common use cases with circular layouts in the domain.
Meyer et al. [33] used a circular adjacent layout for visualizing interconnection between different parts of a sequence.
The adjacent circular arrangement allows the analyst to look at overall connections between sequences in a space-efficient manner.
GenoREC gives preference to empirically backed design guidelines.
When there is a lack of empirical results, GenoREC factors the genomics-specific knowledge for the recommendation.
GenoREC recommends color saturation encoding used for commonly used heatmap visualizations for overview tasks.
There is no conclusive evidence that negates the use of color saturation encoding for overview tasks.
The knowledge for recommendation is represented and stored as a decision matrix in GenoREC’s model.
For each component (C1–C6) in Sect. 6.1.1, there is a distinct decision matrix.
The decision matrix for the Encoding component (C1) is shown in Fig. 5.
The rows in the matrix represent all the possible output options.
The columns in the matrix represent input factors that affect the output selection.
The cells in the matrix represent if the corresponding output (row) can support the corresponding input item (column).
GenoREC encodes the relationship between input and output as a binary value.
A cell with a dark circle represents a value of 1, meaning the output is supported by the corresponding input column.
In the 'Quant.' column (Fig. 5), all the cells corresponding to position (e.g., 'Point'), length (e.g., 'Rect'), and saturation (i.e., 'Saturation') have a value of 1.
Since the hue channel is not used to represent quantitative data, all cells corresponding to the hue channel have a value of 1 (i.e., empty cells).
Representing recommendation knowledge as binary-valued features allows GenoREC to use a similarity computation technique to rank the output of each component (C1–C6).
GenoREC uses the ranking for recommendation.
GenoREC computes the similarity between the input and all the output items in the product matrix using a cosine similarity metric.
The cosine similarity score expects two vectors of equal size and generates a score in the range of [-1,1].
GenoREC’s algorithm generates an input vector for each recommendation component based on the features given in the column headers of the decision matrix.
GenoREC scores the similarity of the input vector with all rows of the decision matrix.
A higher cosine similarity score closer to 1 means that the two vectors are more similar.
A lower cosine similarity score closer to -1 means the two vectors are dissimilar.
These scores are used for ranking in the GenoREC recommendation system.
GenoREC recommends the output item with the highest score.
Fig. 6 shows the steps in GenoREC’s recommendation algorithm.

GenoREC visually encodes each data attribute in the input data.

Qualitative feedback was gathered from domain experts to validate the recommendation output.

This study sought to answer the question: 'Does the output from the recommendation system match experts' expectations?'
Answering this question is important because it validates the recommendation rules applied by GenoREC.
The validation of the recommendation rules ensures that GenoREC's subsequent implementation is valid.
Feedback from this study helped refine GenoREC’s design goals.
Feedback from this study helped improve the user interface and the system’s overall workflow.
Five domain experts were recruited for the formative study.
The participants had experience at the intersection of genomics and visualization ranging from 8–20 years.
The study was designed as a semi-structured interview lasting an hour.
Participants were presented with three different data analysis scenarios in the form of short paragraphs of text.

Participants were asked to describe an appropriate visualization for each scenario.
Participants were asked to use GenoREC and comment on the accuracy of the recommended visualization.
At the end of the interview, participants were encouraged to provide feedback on the user interface.
All responses were analyzed by open coding and thematic analysis.
Most participants found GenoREC’s recommendations accurate and only required minor modifications for the scenarios included in the study.
This feedback led to the export feature in GenoREC’s user interface.

One participant expected the visualizations to include additional biological contexts such as gene annotation track and ideogram plots that provide a summary of chromosomes coupled with genomic location information.

The Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used to measure if the scenario-wise median difference in responses varies between GenoREC and the alternate stimulus.

Qualitative feedback from participants was used to understand why GenoREC performed better than the alternate stimulus.
A linear layout with a focus+context (GenoREC) was compared to a circular layout (alternate) in an identify task.
Some analysts did not like the circular layout based on participant feedback.

An additional reason for preferring GenoREC’s recommendation was the focus+context interaction.

For Scenario 8, GenoREC recommended a visualization stacked alignment.

Users could solve correlation tasks through an overview or a region-based focus approach.

Using subjective responses from domain users presents a practical way of assessing visualization recommendations for genomics.
We present a sequential recommendation model for genomics visualization.
To develop the sequential model, visualization techniques in genomics were broken down into multiple components (e.g., encoding, layout) and order was added to them.
The sequential method can be applied in other domains and visualization techniques.

Tree visualizations can be decomposed into three components based on a visualization taxonomy: 'Representation' (explicit, implicit, hybrid), 'Alignment' (parallel, radial, free), and 'Dimensionality' (2D, 3D, hybrid).
Tree visualization experts can determine the dependencies between components, such as whether 'Representation' of tree visualizations should be determined before 'Dimensionality'.
After ordering the components, domain experts can systematically curate recommendation knowledge for each component and create a sequential recommendation model for tree visualizations.
The sequential model may not apply universally across all domains and visualization techniques.

Applying the sequential model to infographics can be challenging because they offer a lot of design freedom, making it difficult to identify their design space and decompose visualization into smaller components.

Using a sequential model can simplify the process of designing a knowledge-based recommendation model for domains and visualization techniques where it is possible to break down visualization into components and apply order to them.
We anticipate the sequential model to be adopted more in the future.
GenoREC’s recommendation model can be updated by changing each component’s output items and decision factors.
Introducing a new glyph encoding in the Encoding component (C1) requires adding a new row to the decision matrix.
Adding additional decision factors requires adding a new column to the decision matrix of each component.
Factoring in user preferences for recommended encodings involves adding a new column in the decision matrix to store the relationship between encoding output and the user-preference factor.
Component-level changes in GenoREC are straightforward as they do not affect other aspects of the model.
Extending the recommendation model to handle a new component could be challenging.
Adding a new component requires careful analysis of its dependencies with all the other components, which can be complex if done post-hoc.
Researchers are recommended to err on the side of inclusion when identifying the components to be used with GenoREC’s recommendation approach.
GenoREC’s model is currently accessible through the user interface.
The model will be packaged into a library for programmatic access in the future.
The library will enable embedding GenoREC into tools like Gos that generate Gosling specifications through Python, e.g., in Jupyter Notebooks.
It will be possible to generate visualizations based on actual data files rather than descriptions of the files.

User preference in GenoREC’s recommendation model is an interesting direction for future work.
Currently, there is no user preference data for genomics visualizations.
With the adoption of GenoREC, more information on user-preferred visualizations can be collected.
User preference data can be used in the recommendation model for ranking the output.
The recommendation model will be explained to users in the future.
Explanations will justify the reasons behind recommendations to answer domain user questions, e.g., 'Why was a linear layout recommended over a circular layout?'

Our work offers critical guidance for visualization researchers developing similar recommendation systems in other domains.

Our model was implemented using PyTorch with four types of CNN backbones: ResNet-18, ResNet-101, DLA-34, and Hourglass-104.
The Hourglass-104 network was used as the standard backbone.
ResNet-18, ResNet-101, and DLA-34 were modified by using deformable convolution layers.
To evaluate the performance of parsing a circular glyph, we adopted the average precision (AP) value from the precision/recall curve.
The evaluation focused on two tasks: what and where.
Each detection was considered true or false based on the area that overlapped with the ground truth bounding boxes.
Overlap area was calculated using the formula IoU = area(Bp ∩ Bgt) / area(Bp ∪ Bgt), where Bp is the predicted bounding box and Bgt is the ground truth bounding box.
If IoU exceeded a threshold, the detection was considered true.
Without test augmentation, object detection performance was evaluated on the circular glyph dataset containing 8k training images and 2k validation images.
We reported the average precision (AP) over all IoU thresholds, as well as AP at thresholds of 0.5 (AP50) and 0.75 (AP75).
Table 1 shows results with different backbones.
According to the definition, a high AP value denotes a good detection model.
Table 1 reports the average precision of detecting visual elements.
The detection was performed using different backbones in the circular glyph dataset.
The Hourglass-104 DLA-34 backbone achieved an AP of 82.6, $AP_{50}$ of 98.4, $AP_{75}$ of 94.1, and inference time of 92 ms.
The Hourglass-104 DLA-34 backbone achieved an AP of 82.2, $AP_{50}$ of 98.2, $AP_{75}$ of 93.2, and inference time of 45 ms.
The ResNet-101 backbone achieved an AP of 80.8, $AP_{50}$ of 98.1, $AP_{75}$ of 92.7, and inference time of 36 ms.
The ResNet-18 backbone achieved an AP of 79.0, $AP_{50}$ of 97.6, $AP_{75}$ of 91.4, and inference time of 20 ms.
Table 1 shows the results with different backbones.
The running time was tested on a local machine with Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8260 CPU, Tesla V100 GPU, PyTorch 1.5.0, and CUDA 10.2.
All backbones take less than 0.1 seconds to process one image.
Hourglass-104 had the highest accuracy among all backbones with a relatively good speed.
The Hourglass-104 backbone was selected for model training.
This section discusses the implications and limitations of GlyphCreator.
Using AI to aid in data visualization has become more common.
AI is used to simplify the visualization task.
Visualization is used to help in the machine learning task, creating a loop of visualization and AI.
A detection model was trained to automatically deconstruct a circular glyph for the former arrow.
The lack of a training dataset led to the creation of the second arrow.
D3.js was used to draw circular glyphs.
PNGs and annotations were saved as the training dataset.
Simple calculation was utilized as a substitute for the labor-intensive annotation process.
A better model with high accuracy and fast performance is needed for an improved authoring tool benefiting the community.
A comprehensive understanding of the design space of circular glyphs for data visualization is required for a perfect model.
Through multiple iterative rounds, a well-behaved model and a tool, GlyphCreator, with high efficiency were achieved.
GlyphCreator provides a successful work example rooted in two fields of knowledge.
GlyphCreator inspires the development of future visualization tools.
Glyphs use different visual channels to encode multiple informational dimensions.
Glyphs are effective but their complex layouts and multiple encodings can make the design and realization process difficult.
Automating the generation of glyphs is a meaningful task.
Example-based generation is more efficient compared to creating glyphs from scratch.
In real scenarios, users with different design skills in the visualization field can use GlyphCreator.
Users with design expertise usually have a clear goal for their glyph and want to see the final result quickly for iteration.
With GlyphCreator, users with design expertise can see the image only after a few minutes of operation.
Users with design expertise can use the glyph in their system and preview it quickly with GlyphCreator.
Users with little design experience have a clear understanding of glyphs but find the design process difficult.
Users with little design experience want to use an existing glyph as a reference for their own data.
With GlyphCreator, users with little design experience can obtain their desired glyph even when they have little understanding of the original image.
The example-based glyph generation method provides improved efficiency to users who need to design glyphs, even without a complete understanding of the form.
Example-based glyph generation is a useful and effective means of representing multivariate data visualization.
Example-based glyph generation could have a wide range of applications.
Our dataset of circular glyphs can be used for tasks such as predicting visualization types.
Our dataset of circular glyphs can be used for searching for a glyph image using keywords.
For each glyph, we labeled each visual element with its category.
A new model for chart prediction can be feasibly trained for all visual elements in circular glyphs.
People can use the labels in annotations to search for a desired circular glyph by inputting several keywords about the corresponding visual elements.
During the design process, people aim to find a glyph with a particular visual element that is suitable for one data type, like a pie chart for proportional data.
Obtaining content results by inputting related keywords is difficult with popular search engines, such as Google.
With our dataset that contains numerous images, users can acquire related images for inspiration or other possible usages.
GlyphCreator has limited support for glyph style customization.
There is a default style for all users, and users must edit it manually.
A possible solution is improving the model to learn the style parameters of input images, such as color scheme, and automatically configure the generated glyphs.
Our approach was applied only to circular glyphs, but it can potentially be generalized to other glyph types.
By analyzing and exploring the design space of other glyphs, we can extend our dataset and build a model for parsing all kinds of glyphs.
The deconstruction model is not diverse enough to support circular glyphs in other fields.
We collected circular glyphs designed by experts in the visualization field.
Other fields, such as journalism, could use glyphs for data representation, and these glyphs could also be collected for diversity.
The deconstruction model could be utilized for many other images with high accuracy by adopting a dataset with a broadened range.
GlyphCreator is an automatic system for generating circular glyphs based on an example-based method.
Existing circular glyphs were collected to create a design space of circular glyphs.
The design space was used to analyze the relationship among different visual elements.
A circular glyph dataset was built using the design space.
A framework was proposed that includes a deconstruction model to obtain the layout of circular glyphs.
In GlyphCreator, users can bind multi-dimensional data with the layout of circular glyphs in a straightforward manner.
Users can generate a new circular glyph after revising the style using GlyphCreator.
The deconstruction model was evaluated through a quantitative experiment.
The expressiveness and usability of the approach were demonstrated through a usage scenario and user interviews.
The work provides a new idea for automatically generating glyphs in all visualizations via a two-way method, a loop of visualization and AI.
The pipeline will be extended in the future by analyzing other glyphs.
The authoring tools of GlyphCreator will be expanded to support other creative designs.

Visualization authoring libraries and the interfaces they provide can be categorized by their level of abstraction.

On one end of the spectrum, users are provided with graphical elements (e.g., rectangles, circles, and lines) that need to be composed from the bottom up to construct visualizations (e.g., Processing and D3).
This approach is the most expressive way to create a wide variety of visualizations but, at the same time, makes the construction process time-consuming and laborious.
Visualization tools on the opposite end of the spectrum are often called template-based, which provide a list of visualization types that users can select.
Since many design decisions are predetermined and fixed in the templates by developers, template-based tools have shown to be less expressive but more accessible to use.
In the middle of this continuum are tools which have been adopted widely in the visualization community due to their strength in balancing the expressiveness and ease-of-use.

Multiple views can be specified in the nested format for flexible view arrangements (i.e., multiView inside views).
The parallel and serial arrangements position genomic coordinates of multiple views in parallel or series, respectively.
Two linear views are juxtaposed vertically or horizontally in parallel and serial arrangements.
With two circular views, they are combined into concentric views in the parallel or serial arrangement.
In the serial arrangement, two circular views become semi-circular views.
In the parallel arrangement, two circular views are stacked from the inside to the outside of the center.
The vertical and horizontal arrangements juxtapose views horizontally and vertically in the ‘screen space,’ respectively.
In linear views, parallel and serial arrangements are equivalent to vertical and horizontal arrangements.
Multiple circular views would be placed next to each other without becoming concentric.
Users can link views and interactive brushes for synchronous visual exploration.
This enables users to create visualizations that support diverse exploration scenarios.
Examples of exploration scenarios include overview+detail views and comparative visualizations.
view := ..., xLinkingId?
mark := ... | “brush”
x := ..., linkingId?
Views and interactive brushes have their own viewports for browsing genomic intervals.
A viewport is specified in the grammar by linkingId.
LinkingId is similar to Vega’s Signals in that scales of visual channels can be shared using unique identifications.
When multiple views reference the same viewport, they share the same genomic coordinates.
Coordinated zooming and panning interactions across views and/or brushes are possible.
The brush is interactive, allowing users to adjust its left and right edges or position by clicking and dragging.
Semantic zooming is an advanced exploration technique that allows visual elements to be represented differently at different scales.
Previous studies considered aspects to support flexible semantic zooming specifications.
The grammar should support the specification of criteria for determining when to switch between different visual encodings, such as space availability and zoom levels.
Users should be able to define multiple visual encodings for representing the data at different scales.
It should be possible to apply new visual encodings to a complete visualization, such as changing visualization types.
It should be possible to apply new visual encodings to certain visual elements only, such as showing detailed information only to the visual elements that have sufficient space.
Gosling provides control over the visibility of visual marks or an entire track.
The control is achieved through Boolean expressions based on visual properties.
The visual properties include size of tracks, size of marks, or zoom level.
track := ..., visibility?
The visibility is defined by the visibilityCondition.
Threshold is a parameter used to determine a specific cutoff value in a process.
Condition padding refers to the addition of extra data or context to meet certain conditions.
Transition padding involves adding data to facilitate smooth transitions between states or processes.
The target is defined as 'track' or 'mark'.
An operation can be 'less-than' or 'greater-than'.
The measure can be 'width', 'height', or 'zoomLevel'.
The threshold is defined as either a number or the expression |xe-x|.
(conditionPadding | transitionPadding) is defined as a number.

The target of the filter in this approach are visual marks or individual tracks, and logical conditions are expressed by visual properties such as width, height in pixels, and zoom levels in nucleotides.
Users can overlay multiple tracks and define visibility conditions for individual tracks to show and hide visual marks or entire tracks depending on their properties.
Size differences of various patterns in genomes span orders of magnitude, making it infeasible to show individual nucleotides at a genome-wide scale.
Upon zooming far enough into a specific region, it can be useful to see the genome’s nucleotide sequence.

A user can specify a stacked bar chart to show the distribution of nucleotides when zoomed out and overlay an additional track to show individual nucleotides with text labels displayed only when there is enough space to render text marks.
Multiple conditions can be defined in a single track to support flexible visibility criteria, such as determining visibility based on both the size of marks and the zoom level of a track.
In this approach, multiple conditions are combined with logical ‘and’ operations.
The transition between two different visual encodings may be abrupt, which can break a user’s mental map and make exploration less effective.
Gosling supports transitionPadding in the visibility property to avoid abrupt changes.
TransitionPadding adds padding when calculating the conditional operations.
Instead of setting the opacity level of visual marks or tracks to zero or one, a floating number between zero and one is assigned to the opacity.
This approach provides smooth fading across the opacity levels.
For example, if a track is only visible at zoom levels below 40 and specifies a transitionPadding of 10, at zoom level 45, the track’s opacity would be set to 0.5.
The principle of conciseness is applied to make Gosling more accessible to the target audience.
Shortcuts are provided to make the creation of Gosling specifications more efficient.
Gosling provides sensible default values for individual properties based on frequently used visualization types.
Default values include stack for alignment, linear for layout, and vertical for arrangement.
In the hierarchical structure of view and track specifications in Gosling, values defined at higher levels apply to lower levels but can be overridden.
Users can define common properties shared across all views and tracks only once, such as assembly.
Common track properties can be shared across multiple tracks in a single view or inherited from views.
Track-level properties, such as data and encoding, can be defined at the view level, overriding those properties in the tracks of the view.
This approach is especially useful for genomics visualizations where the same encoding is often applied to many tracks.
Gosling.js is a rendering toolkit for Gosling.
Gosling.js uses Gosling specifications in JSON format to create scalable and interactive visualizations on the web.
Gosling.js employs a TypeScript-based definition of the Gosling grammar.
Gosling.js consists of three main components: a compiler, a renderer, and a HiGlass client.
The compiler translates a Gosling specification into a HiGlass-interpretable view configuration.
The HiGlass client interprets the view configuration and fetches the data needed for rendering.
Using the data, the Gosling.js renderer displays individual tracks.
The track renderer is implemented using the Pixi.js WebGL library.
Gosling.js was built on top of the HiGlass infrastructure to access genomic datasets stored in a wide range of file formats.
HiGlass uses a 'tiling' approach for scalable data access, which is employed in common map visualization tools like Google Maps and Open Street Maps.
HiGlass preprocesses data to store aggregated information, such as nearby quantitative values or filtered values, for given genomic regions and resolutions.
The HiGlass client considers the regional information of Gosling.js visualizations, such as genomic regions and zoom levels, and fetches appropriate tiles from the source data.
The HiGlass client passes the fetched tiles to Gosling.js for visualization.
Several data formats, such as Cooler, Vector, and Multivec, require the HiGlass server for more efficient visual exploration.
Many common data formats, such as BAM, BigWig, CSV (including BED and GFF), and JSON, can be used directly in Gosling.js without a dedicated HiGlass server or data pre-processing.

700 lines of code were written using JavaScript with Pixi.js for graphical representations.

We provide a high-level comparison of Gosling to other visualization tools concerning our design principles.
A common limitation of existing tools is the lack of support for both linear and circular layouts.
Vega-Lite currently only supports arc marks for radial visualizations.
It is impossible to create Circos-like visualizations using Vega-Lite.
The multi-scale encoding is not supported in most tools except ggBio.
ggBio only allows switching between encoding templates by zoom level.
ggBio and Circos only support static visualizations.
Users’ ability to explore genomics data across scales is very limited with ggBio and Circos.
Modern genome browsers commonly use template-based approaches which limit their track-level expressiveness.
Generic tools like Vega-Lite and GenomeSpy are more expressive but do not support large and complex genomic datasets well.
GenomeSpy requires users to convert most genomics datasets into tabular formats prior to using them in the system.
Gosling has some practical limitations compared to existing tools.
Some genome browsers support a wider range of genomics data formats, such as SEG and VCF in IGV.js.
GenomeSpy has a well-structured GPU pipeline that allows rendering of a large number of graphical elements more efficiently than currently possible in Gosling.js.
Vega-Lite and ggBio are integrated into computational analysis environments, such as R or Python.
The Grammar of Graphics decomposes visualizations into abstracted components.
Data needs to be stored in an abstracted and consistent format, such as a tabular format, to facilitate the Grammar of Graphics approach.
Genomics data is stored in a wide range of text-based, binary, or compressed file formats, many of which are not tabular.
Grammars that expect tabular data require users to convert their data before visualizing it, which is inefficient and often not feasible.
The need for data conversion creates a conflict between domain specificity and data scalability.
Asking users to perform data transformation simplifies the rendering process of the grammar but places an enormous burden on users.
Data visualization software is typically employed in genomics data analysis alongside many other analysis tools in an iterative fashion.
Requiring users to convert gigabytes of data for each tool is unrealistic.

If the grammar supports domain-specific file formats and can transform data into tabular formats on the fly before encoding, domain specificity and data scalability can be addressed without burdening users.
On-the-fly data transformation is computationally expensive or impractical for large and complex genomics datasets, leading to data scalability issues.
This represents a significant barrier for developing domain-specific visualization grammars for domains dealing with large and complex data like genomics.
The HiGlass data visualization infrastructure allowed us to overcome the trade-off between domain specificity and data scalability.
HiGlass provides support for diverse genomics file formats, increasing domain specificity.
HiGlass supports pre-aggregated, tiled datasets for efficient rendering in Gosling.js, increasing data scalability.
Gosling is designed to enable effective visual exploration of genomics data.
Support for multi-scale exploration is critical for effective navigation of genomic datasets.
Users can author interactive visualizations, such as coordinated multiple views with zooming and panning interactions.
Exploration of genomics data is more effective if additional interactive components are integrated with visualization.

A common scenario is to link a visualization to a data table that lists additional information about the visualized data records, such as genes and their locations, possibly ranked by one or more scores.
Using such an interface, users can navigate the data more efficiently by selecting an item in the table to navigate to a specific genomic location.
It is essential to consider appropriate APIs in Gosling.js to integrate visualizations with external components better.
Gosling supports the creation of a wide range of genomic visualization techniques captured in the taxonomy of Nusrat et al.
Gosling currently lacks support for space-filling curves and spatial 3D layouts.
Mapping the genome sequence onto a space-filling curve, such as a Hilbert curve, can produce a compact overview of the genome.
Some examples have been published where the genome was mapped onto simulated 3D spatial coordinates to visualize genome folding and illustrate genome plasticity.
The Gosling grammar can be extended to support space-filling and 3D layouts.
The utility of space-filling and 3D layouts in the context of a grammar is limited as they do not afford alignment with other tracks.
Gosling currently only supports mapping to the entire genome sequence and does not support sequence abstraction.
Sequence abstraction would allow filtering out regions, such as intragenic regions, or scaling genomic regions of different lengths to a unit length.
We intend to add support for sequence abstraction in the future.
We plan to conduct a controlled user study with members of our target audience to assess the grammar’s learnability and overall ease-of-use.
Gosling is a grammar-based toolkit for scalable and interactive genomics data visualization.
Gosling balances expressiveness for multi-scale and multifocus visualizations.
Gosling ensures accessibility for a broad user audience.
The goal was to address the shortcomings of existing approaches for genomics visualization, particularly concerning customizability.
The capabilities of the grammar and the proposed toolkit were demonstrated through a series of examples.
The examples represent the wide spectrum of visual representations and interactions supported by Gosling.
Developing a domain-specific grammar and an accompanying toolkit can potentially overcome several critical limitations of general-purpose visualization grammars.
This work encourages the development of visualization grammars for other domains with unique domain-specific data types, visual representations, and analysis tasks.
Gosling will enable notable progress in genomics data visualization by providing a foundation for the design of novel scalable, interactive, multi-view visualizations.
Gosling removes common barriers such as limited expressiveness of template-based approaches and data scalability.
Gosling will enable broader participation in visualization design and implementation in genomics.
The success of visualization grammars in other fields suggests that this work will serve as the foundation of an ecosystem of tools built around Gosling and Gosling.js.

Plasmids play a central role in bacterial adaptation and in the dissemination of antimicrobial resistance.
There is a growing need for accessible tools that support plasmid comparative analysis without requiring local computational infrastructure.
Several circular genome visualization platforms exist, but most are designed for general bacterial genome analysis rather than focused on plasmid comparison.
Host element reference-based aligner (HERA) is a web server for intuitive visualization and comparison of plasmids and other circular molecules through BLAST alignment against reference sequences.
HERA is built on interactive circular genome visualization.

HERA simplifies comparative genomics by providing an accessible interface for exploring sequence similarity, identifying conserved regions, and analyzing genetic elements without the complexity of traditional local tools.

HERA includes a plasmid-oriented annotation pipeline covering replicon and mobility typing, antimicrobial resistance detection, mobile element identification, and homology search against the PLSDB plasmid database.
HERA provides an automatic selection of the reference which is the most appropriate from the uploaded sequences.
The web server is available without login or any restriction at https://web.ccb.uni-saarland.de/hera/.

Rendering circular images in common visualization packages like ggplot is inherently difficult.
Several tools have been developed to address the challenges of rendering circular images, each with distinct capabilities and limitations.
Circos is a flexible framework capable of rendering complex multi-track plots with ribbon and link diagrams connecting genomic positions.
Circos is Perl-dependent and offers no graphical user interface.
GenoVi created a Python command-line wrapper around Circos to improve accessibility.

The CGView Comparison Tool is command-line-driven, produces only static images, and requires installation of multiple dependencies including Perl, Java, and BLAST.

BRIG (BLAST Ring Image Generator) addressed usability challenges by providing a cross-platform Java desktop application with a graphical user interface for generating circular BLAST comparison images.
